summary:
Ankit Jain, co-founder of Aviator, argues that line-by-line code review is already over and that what replaced it — AI writes code, AI reviews code in the GitHub UI, humans skim and merge — is the wrong configuration, with over 30% of changes now merging unreviewed and median review wait roughly quadrupled. He corrects his earlier five-layer trust model: it captured correctness and semantic accuracy but missed that review is fundamentally about alignment — knowledge sharing, mentorship, architectural feedback, onboarding, and collaboration — and that half must survive.

He rejects front-loaded spec-driven development as a fix because a frozen spec is the 1970s waterfall model with no feedback loop, and LLMs are non-deterministic and make their own decisions during implementation. The real intent lives in the back-and-forth between developer and agent in sessions like Cloud Code, Codex, or Cursor — and those prompts are thrown away the moment a PR opens.

His proposal combines two pieces. An AI slop registry captures recurring review comments and codifies them as auto-applied guardrails, so humans stop repeating the same feedback. A verification loop captures the session's user decisions as acceptance criteria, combines them with registry invariants to generate a test plan, and runs it deterministically against a live preview (with LLMs as fallback). Crucially, the test plan must be built from the session, not the code — if the same agent that wrote the code also writes the test plan, it will not catch its own issues. The human review surface then becomes intent (architectural discussions about data models and service interactions) plus evidence (criteria, test results, screenshots), closer to behavior-driven development than TDD.

He closes with homework: mine your last 1,000 review comments to seed the registry, accept that adoption follows a J-curve of upfront pain, and remember that code review is not just about code review — it is about getting alignment. He invites the audience to pilot Aviator's new product, Verify.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: The five-layer trust model, and what it got wrong
sections.summary: Ankit recaps the five-layer trust model he published on LinkedIn a few months earlier. He concedes it got one thing wrong: it focused on building trust for correctness but completely missed the alignment half of review — knowledge sharing, mentorship, architectural feedback, and onboarding — which is the most important part of release in team settings.

sections.title: We already stopped reviewing, and AI reviews nobody reads
sections.summary: He argues the debate about when we stop reading code line by line is already over because we have stopped: 861% code churn, median review time roughly quadrupled, incidents-to-PR ratio rising, and over 30% of changes merge with no review. When an AI agent writes the code and another AI agent reviews it inside the GitHub UI, humans only skim and merge — what he calls 'the wrong thing configured.'

sections.title: What code review was actually for
sections.summary: He traces formal code review back roughly 15–20 years (Google's Mondrian in 2006) and argues review is not just about catching bugs, conventions, and security. It is also about alignment — knowledge sharing, mentorship, architectural feedback, onboarding, and collaboration — and that half must survive even when tooling handles semantic accuracy.

sections.title: Spec-driven development is waterfall again
sections.summary: He critiques front-loaded spec-driven development as a fix: requirements → spec → implement → verify is the 1970s waterfall model with no feedback loop. Since LLMs are non-deterministic and make their own decisions during implementation, a frozen spec falls short in day-to-day software development. The intent does not only live in the spec; it also lives in Jira tickets, PRDs, and most importantly in the prompts.

sections.title: Intent lives in the prompts, which we throw away
sections.summary: The real decisions are made during the back-and-forth between developer and agent in sessions like Cloud Code, Codex, or Cursor. But the moment a PR opens, those prompts — and the decisions in them — are thrown away, which is one of the things his proposal explicitly tries to change.

sections.title: The AI slop registry
sections.summary: Introduced as the answer to the remaining 'who catches the bugs?' question. The registry captures recurring review comments and codifies them as guardrails that are auto-applied to future changes. Over time it acts like additional training on top of the base LLM, and every recurring comment becomes a guardrail humans no longer have to re-review.

sections.title: Session to acceptance criteria to test plan
sections.summary: He ties alignment and semantic accuracy into one loop: capture the coding session's user responses as acceptance criteria, combine those with the AI slop registry invariants to produce a test plan, and run that test plan via a verification system against a live preview. The human review surface becomes intent and evidence (criteria + test results), not the diff — closer to behavior-driven development than TDD, with criteria and invariants written in English so PMs and designers can participate.

sections.title: Deterministic where you can, and reviewing intent not the diff
sections.summary: He closes by clarifying the system is not supposed to be perfect: be deterministic where you can and use LLMs as fallback where you must. Example given — adding a payment form to a web app: an AI agent browses the preview, fills the form, captures screenshots and database snapshots, and checks the criteria. Screenshot/sanity testing can still be done by agents, but reviewers now look at solid evidence of intent being met rather than line-by-line code.

sections.title: Build the test plan from the session, not the code
sections.summary: He stresses that the test plan must be derived from the captured session — what was said to build, what was tried and rejected — rather than from the code itself. If the same agent that wrote the code also writes the test plan, it will not produce a test plan that catches its own issues, the same failure mode Dex discussed the previous day. Capturing session context is therefore the key input.

sections.title: Reviewing intent and evidence: architecture above the diff
sections.summary: Because the verification loop captures the intent and produces evidence, reviewers move one level up: instead of reading line by line they discuss architectural decisions — how data models are created, how services interact. That is where collaboration happens, while the diff itself is no longer the review surface.

sections.title: Homework: mine 1,000 comments; J-curve; alignment is the point
sections.summary: He gives the audience a concrete homework assignment: mine the last 1,000 review comments and build an AI slop registry from the recurring ones. The registry compounds with every merged PR, codifies best practices, maintains semantic accuracy, and preserves the collaboration half of review. Adoption follows a J-curve — building the registry is upfront pain that pays off over time — and he invites the audience to pilot Aviator's new product Verify. His parting reminder: code review is not just about code review, it is about getting alignment.

demonstrations: Earlier walkthrough of a coding session (Cloud Code / Codex / Cursor) captured, converted into acceptance criteria via LLM, combined with registry invariants into a test plan, and run against a preview.
Example of changing a web app to add a payment form: a test plan is created, an AI agent browses the preview, fills the form, captures screenshots and database snapshots as evidence.
Reviewers now discuss architecture (data models, service interactions) and examine verification evidence instead of reading the diff line by line.
limitations: LLMs are not deterministic, so they make their own decisions during implementation that the front-loaded spec does not capture.
AI reviewers are imperfect and miss issues that human reviewers would catch.
Not every check can be made deterministic; LLM-based checks are needed as fallback for things like visual or exploratory verification.
If the same agent that wrote the code also writes the test plan, it will not build a test plan that catches issues — test plans must come from session context.
The framework assumes team collaboration — it does not apply to solo 'dark factory' workflows with no human reviewers.
Adoption follows a J-curve: building the registry takes upfront time before payoff compounds.
quantitativeClaims: Median review time has increased by roughly 4x compared with before.
Over 30% of changes are merged without any review at all.
Formal code review as a practice dates back roughly 15–20 years, with Google's internal Mondrian launching in 2006.
Homework suggestion: mine your last 1,000 review comments to seed the registry.
